copy.headline: Danish ID number no longer proves identity after data on 8.8 million people is taken

extended.text: The CPR number, Denmark's personal identity number, can no longer be trusted to identify anyone, the Agency for Societal Security said on Tuesday. Over ten days in September, unauthorised people harvested data on 8.8 million people from the CPR register.

'You can no longer count on having identified a specific citizen if you are given a CPR number,' said Laila Reenberg, the agency's director. Companies should use MitID or another two-factor login, or a one-time code by text or email. Pharmacies may ask customers for ID or security questions before handing out medicine.

The data was taken through the legal access of a small Danish company, which the authorities will not name. Each search of the register is billed, and an unusually large invoice gave the theft away. Mainly names and addresses were taken, said Mikkel Leihardt, a head of department at the digitalisation ministry.
Investigators do not yet know who is behind it, and no one has been charged. Christina Egelund, the digitalisation minister, has ordered a security review of the whole register.

copy.headline: Frederiksen promises Ukraine full support but says Denmark has no money to spare

standard.text: Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, promised Denmark's 'full-throated support for Ukraine' in her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, on Tuesday. 'Russia does not want peace, the Kremlin wants new land,' she said.

Payments from the Ukraine Fund, which the government set up when the war began, have fallen since 2023; only 4.4 billion kroner has been set aside this year. Asked by Kristeligt Dagblad how the support would continue, Frederiksen said no country in Europe has much money to spare. 'Neither do we,' she said.
Altinget writes that she could as well have given the speech as head of a Social Democratic government of her own.

short.text: Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, promised 'full-throated support for Ukraine' in her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, on Tuesday. Asked by Kristeligt Dagblad how, she said no country in Europe has much money to spare. 'Neither do we,' she said.

copy.headline: Denmark's outgoing Speaker says he has 'powerful enemies' in his own party

standard.text: Søren Gade, who left the post of Speaker of Denmark's parliament on Tuesday, says he has 'powerful enemies in Venstre', a liberal party and his own. He was answering a portrait in Jyllands-Posten, a Danish daily newspaper, in which 13 anonymous sources called him vain, disloyal, selfish, lazy and greedy.

Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, called anonymous attacks by elected politicians 'beneath contempt'; Troels Lund Poulsen, Venstre's leader, called the piece 'an unusually sad and nasty portrait'.
The newspaper amended the portrait on Tuesday, saying its first version was 'not sufficiently balanced'; its political editor stands '100 per cent' behind the original.

short.text: Søren Gade, who left the post of Speaker of Denmark's parliament on Tuesday, says he has 'powerful enemies in Venstre', a liberal party and his own. Jyllands-Posten, a Danish daily newspaper, had printed a portrait in which 13 anonymous sources called him vain and lazy; it has since amended it.

copy.deck: A newspaper portrait built on 13 anonymous sources called him vain and lazy; the prime minister calls such attacks 'beneath contempt'.

copy.headline: Germany arrests a former spy chief on suspicion of treason

standard.text: August Hanning, head of the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of spying against the German state, passing on state secrets and attempted treason. Germany's federal prosecutors say he also worked as an agent for a foreign intelligence service.

A former department head under Hanning, who left the BND this spring, was arrested too. Prosecutors suspect he passed Hanning about 2,000 documents between 2010 and June 2022, which Hanning used to write a security analysis for a foreign service.
A kidnapping attempt in South Jutland in 2022 put police on the case. Hanning is also accused of sending mercenaries to Denmark to abduct two children.

short.text: August Hanning, head of the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of spying and attempted treason. Federal prosecutors say a former subordinate passed him about 2,000 documents. A kidnapping attempt in South Jutland in 2022 put police on the case.

copy.deck: August Hanning ran the foreign intelligence service from 1998 to 2005; a kidnapping attempt in South Jutland put police on his trail.

copy.headline: Government plans 900 million kroner for schools after historically weak test results

standard.text: The government will set aside 900 million kroner for public schools in its 2027 budget proposal, four ministers told Politiken. Of that, 200 million goes to 100 schools where pupils do particularly badly in Danish and maths, 200 million to small rural schools and 500 million to schools generally.
It follows a Pisa survey, which about a month ago found 15-year-olds historically weak in science, maths and reading.
The government wants more teachers, such as more lessons taught by two, but plans no pay rise. 'I personally think we should look elsewhere,' Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, told DR.
Gordon Ørskov Madsen, chairman of the teachers' union, called it 'very positive'.

short.text: The government will set aside 900 million kroner for public schools in its 2027 budget proposal, four ministers told Politiken, 200 million of it for 100 schools where pupils do particularly badly in Danish and maths.
